text:
Entities never live alone. Customers matter because they place orders. And orders matter because they contain products. So if entities are the nouns, relationships are the verbs. And a good one reads like a sentence. Customer places order says more than customer has order.

Zoom in, and that line is really rows linking to rows. Ada's row links to orders one oh one and one oh two. Grace's, to one oh three. Postgres keeps each link as a key. Every order just carries its customer's id. The relationship is the idea... and the foreign key is how the database holds on to it. But a bare line leaves a big question open. How many?

That's cardinality, and you ask it both ways. One customer, how many orders? Zero, one, or many. One order, how many customers? Exactly one. That's one-to-many, and the key sits on the many side. Two orders, both storing Ada's id.

Crow's-foot notation draws those answers right onto the line. Every end gets two marks. Next to the box is the most. A bar means one, and a crow's foot means many. Farther out is the least. A circle means zero, and a bar means one. Two bars, exactly one. A profile belongs to one user. A bar and a circle, zero or one. An employee gets one parking pass, at most. A foot and a bar, one or many. An order holds at least one item. A foot and a circle, zero or many. A customer might not have ordered yet. And feet at both ends? That's many-to-many, like students and courses.

And those marks change the schema. Many devices per employee? Then device rows can share an employee id. But one badge, at most? Then no employee id can show up twice. Give Ada a second badge... and Postgres says NO. It never sees your picture. You translate it, into keys and constraints.
